questions.topic: Trainee hospital ADD stocking: independently transported CIII–VI versus prohibited CII
questions.actor: licensed pharmacy technician trainee; hospital pharmacist
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital with an on-site licensed pharmacy uses an Automated Dispensing Device (ADD) on its inpatient floor at the address on the hospital MCSR. A Board-licensed pharmacy technician trainee (PTT) completed the facility's ADD
questions.legal_decision: PTT can handle verified CIII–VI ADD stock without direct visual pharmacist supervision, but cannot use that privilege for CII.
questions.critical_exception: Hospital on-site pharmacy; device at hospital MCSR address; original pharmacy verification completed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If this worker instead held an ordinary Massachusetts pharmacy technician license and was directly pharmacist-supervised, CII loading could fall under the different Policy §IV pathway.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital with an on-site licensed pharmacy uses an Automated Dispensing Device (ADD) on its inpatient floor at the address on the hospital MCSR. A Board-licensed pharmacy technician trainee (PTT) completed the facility's ADD training. Pharmacy staff already verified sealed Schedule IV and Schedule II packages. Under the 2023-08 joint stocking policy, which trainee activities are authorized WITHOUT a pharmacist directly observing the ADD loading, assuming the required barcode process? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Transport and load the pharmacist-verified Schedule IV package into the patient-care ADD under the direction and supervision of a pharmacist.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2023-08 §III permits PTTs to transport and load already pharmacist-verified Schedule III–VI medications without direct pharmacist supervision, while still under pharmacist direction and supervision.

choices.text: Transport and load the pharmacist-verified Schedule II package without direct pharmacist supervision merely because the trainee completed the same training.
choices.why: Incorrect. The PTT exception in §III is restricted to Schedules III–VI, not Schedule II.

choices.text: Use electronic validation to verify the expiration date and remove expired Schedule IV stock from that ADD.
choices.why: Correct. Policy §III also permits PTTs to check expiry and remove expired Schedule III–VI stock using barcode or equivalent electronic validation.

choices.text: Independently verify and dispense an unreviewed Schedule IV patient-specific order from the ADD.
choices.why: Incorrect. The stocking policy does not grant the trainee independent clinical validation or dispensing authority.

choices.text: Treat the trainee as a certified pharmacy technician for Schedule II loading based on having the manager's verbal approval alone.
choices.why: Incorrect. Licensed PTT status does not convert to a licensed technician or certified technician scope.

questions.topic: Certified tech inventory-system to ADD exception: ordinary SVI versus gabapentin
questions.actor: licensed nationally certified technician; inpatient pharmacist
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts nationally certified licensed pharmacy technician works in a hospital pharmacy. Using an approved electronic inventory system and barcode checks, the technician intends to pull a sealed manufacturer carton of gabapentin (Mas
questions.legal_decision: Reject no-prior-pharmacist-verification certified-tech stock selection of PMP-designated Schedule VI gabapentin.
questions.critical_exception: Gabapentin is Massachusetts Schedule VI but explicitly excluded from the limited unverified-stock exception.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the drug were ordinary sealed, non-PMP-reportable Schedule VI stock and other electronic validation safeguards were met, the technician could use the §V stocking pathway.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts nationally certified licensed pharmacy technician works in a hospital pharmacy. Using an approved electronic inventory system and barcode checks, the technician intends to pull a sealed manufacturer carton of gabapentin (Massachusetts Schedule VI, designated a PMP-reportable drug) for direct loading into an inpatient ADD. No pharmacist has verified this particular stock selection. The technician cites the joint 2023-08 policy permitting some certified technicians to select Schedule VI medicines without prior pharmacist verification. What is the correct decision?

choices.text: Allow independent selection because all Schedule VI medications qualify for the certified-tech exception regardless of PMP status.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2023-08 §V explicitly excludes PMP-designated drugs, including gabapentin, from the no-prior-pharmacist-verification exception.

choices.text: Change gabapentin's inventory classification to Schedule IV so that the policy's limited Schedule VI restriction disappears.
choices.why: Incorrect. Reclassifying drug records cannot create authorization for staff duties.

choices.text: Permit the technician to select any medication without electronic verification when the manufacturer's container appears intact.
choices.why: Incorrect. The §V exception requires barcode scanning or other electronic validation and no further manipulation.

choices.text: Obtain required pharmacist verification or use another properly supervised authorized stocking route; do not use the §V unverified Schedule VI exception for gabapentin.
choices.why: Correct. The limited exception is for non-patient-specific, non-PMP Schedule VI medications in sealed packaging, not gabapentin.

choices.text: The technician can satisfy the exemption by checking an outpatient prescription's refill count instead of confirming the inventory's PMP exclusion.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescription refill records do not substitute for the policy's non-PMP inventory prerequisite.

questions.topic: Retail pharmacy emergency ADD: nurse loading versus uncertified trainee
questions.trigger: A licensed retail pharmacy provides an approved Automated Dispensing Device (ADD) for an emergency-medication kit in a Massachusetts-licensed healthcare facility. Under Joint Policy 2019-02, the pharmacy must appoint staff to load the devic
questions.legal_decision: Authorize nurse or pharmacist to stock emergency kit ADD under joint policy; reject PTT CII equivalence.
questions.critical_exception: Retail pharmacy emergency kit ADD, not routine pharmacy retail dispensing or inpatient PTT self-directed CII loading.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the stock consisted only of CIII–VI, an ordinary licensed technician could satisfy the separate §10(a) schedule-limited stocking category.
questions.stem: A licensed retail pharmacy provides an approved Automated Dispensing Device (ADD) for an emergency-medication kit in a Massachusetts-licensed healthcare facility. Under Joint Policy 2019-02, the pharmacy must appoint staff to load the device. A licensed nurse, a registered pharmacy technician trainee, and a registered pharmacist are available. Assume the approved kit and facility requirements are satisfied. Which staffing statements are supported? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Any unlicensed clerk can load every federally scheduled substance into the emergency ADD if a patient needs rapid access.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2019-02 §10 lists permissible loading roles; it does not authorize arbitrary unlicensed workers.

choices.text: A licensed nurse is an explicitly permitted professional to load a retail-pharmacy ADD used for emergency kits.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2019-02 §10(b) expressly lists a licensed nurse for this type of ADD.

choices.text: A pharmacy technician trainee is automatically equivalent to a certified technician for loading Schedule II emergency-stock medicine.
choices.why: Incorrect. The 2019-02 loading rule does not grant PTTs certified-tech authority for CII stock.

choices.text: A pharmacist is one of the professions expressly permitted to load the retail emergency-kit ADD.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2019-02 §10(a) expressly includes a pharmacist.

choices.text: A licensed noncertified pharmacy technician can load any Schedule II item without further limits because the ADD is used for emergency care.
choices.why: Incorrect. In §10(a) ordinary pharmacy technicians are expressly limited to Schedule III–VI when stocking these ADDs.

questions.topic: Former nurse still has hospital ADD permissions: revoke unauthorized access
questions.actor: hospital pharmacist; nursing supervisor; system administrator
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy maintains a floor Automated Dispensing Device containing Schedules II–VI for patient-specific medication orders. A former nurse resigned two weeks ago but the ADD still accepts that former employee's login.
questions.legal_decision: Revoke a former employee's ADD access and keep authorized-user list current.
questions.critical_exception: Former worker is no longer authorized, regardless of professional license validity.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the individual remained employed, appropriately licensed and affirmatively authorized for the required clinical role, permitted user access might be maintained.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy maintains a floor Automated Dispensing Device containing Schedules II–VI for patient-specific medication orders. A former nurse resigned two weeks ago but the ADD still accepts that former employee's login. There is no allegation of theft, and all patient medication orders are otherwise valid. The hospital says access need only be reviewed after the annual security inspection. What should the pharmacy and facility do?

choices.text: Maintain the former nurse's active ADD permissions as long as their clinical nursing license has not expired.
choices.why: Incorrect. Policy 2019-02 §5 limits access to authorized licensed personnel, and employment/authorization must still be current.

choices.text: Give the former nurse's credentials to the incoming nurse so no system adjustment is necessary.
choices.why: Incorrect. Credential sharing destroys the required person-specific access control and auditability.

choices.text: Require every licensed nurse to have unrestricted access to all ADD inventory regardless of current job responsibilities.
choices.why: Incorrect. Licensed professional status alone does not establish authorization for every ADD.

choices.text: Delete the device's access logs permanently so that past login permissions cannot be audited by managers.
choices.why: Incorrect. The policy requires accountability and appropriate security/QA controls, not deletion of logs.

choices.text: Immediately remove obsolete access rights and review authorized ADD users under the facility's access-control policy.
choices.why: Correct. Policy 2019-02 §5 limits device access to authorized licensed personnel and requires the list of users to be periodically reviewed and updated.

questions.topic: Cashier detects dispensing QRE: immediately escalate, pharmacist documents within 24 hours
questions.trigger: A nonlicensed front-end cashier learns that a customer received another patient's prescription bag and has already left. The cashier can reach the on-duty pharmacist immediately. The pharmacist initially proposes making a note at the end of
questions.legal_decision: Escalate QRE immediately from nonlicensed staff, notify patient/act, document within 24h.
questions.critical_exception: QRE discovered by cashier with pharmacist available, no serious injury reported, separate 20.02 event trigger not established.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a pharmacist learned of a QRE for the first time several days later, the initial 24-hour documentation clock starts at pharmacist discovery/notification, though staff failure to immediately escalate would remain a violation.
questions.stem: A nonlicensed front-end cashier learns that a customer received another patient's prescription bag and has already left. The cashier can reach the on-duty pharmacist immediately. The pharmacist initially proposes making a note at the end of the week, since no injury has yet been reported. Under 247 CMR 15.03, which actions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The cashier must immediately bring the suspected quality-related event to the pharmacist on duty or MOR.
choices.why: Correct. Section 15.03(1) requires all pharmacy personnel to report discovered QREs to a pharmacist or MOR immediately.

choices.text: Only a licensed technician may notify the pharmacist of a QRE; cashier reports are not authorized.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation says all pharmacy personnel must be trained to bring a QRE to pharmacist attention.

choices.text: The informed pharmacist must promptly address patient notification and appropriate corrective directions to limit harm.
choices.why: Correct. Section 15.03(1)(a)–(c) prescribes immediate notification and error-correction/minimization duties.

choices.text: An absent injury finding removes any need to record or investigate the incorrect patient handoff.
choices.why: Incorrect. Potential patient exposure via wrong-patient dispensing is a QRE requiring response even if injury is not yet known.

choices.text: The pharmacist must initially document the QRE no later than 24 hours after learning about it.
choices.why: Correct. Section 15.03(2)(a) requires initial pharmacist documentation within 24 hours of discovery or notification.

questions.topic: Wholesaler temporary warehouse labor untrained in cold-chain inspection
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts-licensed wholesale druggist hires temporary warehouse workers to receive temperature-sensitive prescription medicines. The employees have never been trained in product storage conditions, shipment damage recognition or the s
questions.legal_decision: Assign qualified/trained people to wholesale receipt/handling tasks; do not permit untrained independent work.
questions.critical_exception: Temporary workers lack task-specific training and experience, goods are sensitive to conditions.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the workers had documented adequate function-specific qualifications and met supervision/process requirements, the staffing defect would be resolved.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts-licensed wholesale druggist hires temporary warehouse workers to receive temperature-sensitive prescription medicines. The employees have never been trained in product storage conditions, shipment damage recognition or the site's controlled access procedures. Management plans to give them independent receipt and disposition authority immediately, saying wholesaler employees do not fall under professional pharmacy rules. What does 247 CMR 7.02 require?

choices.text: Permit independent handling because the only staff requiring pharmaceutical training are pharmacists assigned to retail patient dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 7.02(9) establishes qualifications for each person performing any prescription-drug wholesale distribution activity.

choices.text: Ensure each worker has sufficient education, training or experience for the assigned distribution function before granting unsupervised responsibility.
choices.why: Correct. Section 7.02(9) makes adequate task-specific education, training or experience a condition of the wholesale license.

choices.text: Accept temperature-sensitive shipments without inspection while each worker waits for a future annual retail pharmacist training day.
choices.why: Incorrect. The distributor has immediate product quality/security duties, including receiving inspection under 7.04(4).

choices.text: Convert all incoming prescription medicine to nonprescription goods in the warehouse system to bypass worker qualifications.
choices.why: Incorrect. A warehouse designation cannot remove underlying prescription-drug distribution law.

choices.text: Rely on a signed staff confidentiality agreement alone as proof of training for drug quality, security and distribution records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Confidentiality paperwork is not the functional competence required by 7.02(9).

questions.topic: Liquid outpatient prescription leaves pharmacy without a suitable measuring device
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy fills an oral liquid antibiotic for a toddler. The caregiver asks how to measure each 3.5-mL dose and says they only have an ordinary kitchen tablespoon at home. The dispensing pharmacist plans to place th
questions.legal_decision: Provide/recommend an accurate measuring device with an oral liquid medication at handoff.
questions.critical_exception: Liquid medication with 3.5-mL directions; kitchen spoon is unsuitable.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a suitable marked oral syringe were already supplied or appropriately recommended, the specified measuring-device duty would be met.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy fills an oral liquid antibiotic for a toddler. The caregiver asks how to measure each 3.5-mL dose and says they only have an ordinary kitchen tablespoon at home. The dispensing pharmacist plans to place the bottle in the pickup bag without supplying or recommending a dosing instrument because the prescriber wrote the dose in milliliters. What action meets 247 CMR 9.18?

choices.text: Tell the caregiver to estimate a fraction of the kitchen tablespoon because it is already available in the home.
choices.why: Incorrect. A household spoon is not a reliable properly graduated measuring device for the prescribed milliliter dose.

choices.text: Do not advise about any dosing tool because an oral liquid prescription is exempt from pharmacist dispensing counseling duties.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.18(9) expressly places a proper measuring-device supply or recommendation duty on the pharmacist/pharmacy.

choices.text: Dispense or recommend a suitable graduated device for measuring the prescribed liquid dose and explain proper use as appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.18(9) expressly requires the pharmacy and pharmacist to dispense or recommend a proper measuring device with all liquid medications.

choices.text: Change the directions to 'one tablespoon' without contacting the prescriber in order to avoid calculating the appropriate device.
choices.why: Incorrect. Changing dose instructions without lawful authority can cause medication error and does not satisfy the original intended dose.

choices.text: Ask the caregiver to return after finishing the antibiotic course for a measuring device.
choices.why: Incorrect. Proper measurement is needed for the current therapy, not after treatment.

questions.topic: Hospital discharge prescription greater than 14 days: smallest manufacturer package exception
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy without a retail Drug Store Pharmacy license receives a valid discharge prescription for a noncontrolled medicine. The drug is routinely available through community retail pharmacies, but the manufacturer s
questions.legal_decision: Permit manufacturer smallest 28-day pack under the hospital discharge exception where no smaller manufacturer quantity is sold.
questions.critical_exception: Drug routinely retail available, but only manufacturer unit-of-use presentation exceeds 14 days.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the drug were available from its manufacturer in a 7- or 14-day quantity, the 28-day manufacturer's-package exception would not apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy without a retail Drug Store Pharmacy license receives a valid discharge prescription for a noncontrolled medicine. The drug is routinely available through community retail pharmacies, but the manufacturer supplies this exact product only as a sealed 28-day unit-of-use carton; the pharmacist cannot dispense a smaller manufacturer package. The prescriber ordered 28 days, no refills. The hospital administrator says the discharge quantity is necessarily prohibited because it exceeds 14 days. Which response follows 105 CMR 722.090(B)?

choices.text: The hospital may dispense exactly 14 days after opening the carton, regardless of whether the package is suitable for subdivision.
choices.why: Incorrect. The special rule recognizes medicines available only in manufacturer package sizes larger than 14 days; compulsory splitting is not its categorical instruction.

choices.text: The hospital may dispense a six-month supply because any manufacturer's package size completely eliminates discharge dispensing limits.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception permits only the smallest available manufacturer quantity when larger than 14 days, not any desired quantity.

choices.text: The pharmacy must issue a routine outpatient refill to supply the second 14 days under the same discharge prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 722.090(B)(1) prohibits hospital-pharmacy refills of ED and discharge prescriptions under this route.

choices.text: The hospital pharmacy may dispense the smallest manufacturer-available 28-day carton as a specific exception to the 14-day limit.
choices.why: Correct. Section 722.090(B)(2) allows a larger-than-14-day manufacturer minimum package up to the smallest quantity supplied by the manufacturer.

choices.text: A retail pharmacy must dispense the product because every hospital discharge prescription exceeding 14 days is invalid regardless of package availability.
choices.why: Incorrect. The provision expressly establishes a manufacturer-size exception.

questions.topic: Hospital discharge medicine unavailable at retail: full quantity not automatic refill
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy receives an authentic prescription for an ED discharge patient. The prescribed product is not available from any retail pharmacy, but is lawfully stocked at the hospital. The physician writes an initial 35-
questions.legal_decision: Dispense actual initial prescribed quantity of a drug not available in retail pharmacies under subsection C, with ordinary validity checks.
questions.critical_exception: Drug is genuinely unavailable in retail pharmacies; it is not merely an unavailable brand at the hospital.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the drug were available at ordinary retail pharmacies and no manufacturer minimum-size exception applied, the usual 14-day ED/discharge cap would control.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy receives an authentic prescription for an ED discharge patient. The prescribed product is not available from any retail pharmacy, but is lawfully stocked at the hospital. The physician writes an initial 35-day course, no refills. All other requirements are met. Which conclusions follow 105 CMR 722.090? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The hospital pharmacy can dispense the entire prescribed initial quantity when the drug is not available in retail pharmacies.
choices.why: Correct. Section 722.090(C) permits the amount prescribed for ED or discharge drugs unavailable from a retail pharmacy, notwithstanding the ordinary 14-day limit.

choices.text: The original 14-day supply limit applies without exception even when the product is unavailable in retail pharmacies.
choices.why: Incorrect. Subsection (C) creates the explicit unavailability exception.

choices.text: The exception automatically converts every future 35-day renewal request into a lawful refill under the original order.
choices.why: Incorrect. The exception concerns the prescribed initial quantity; ordinary scope, validity and any applicable refill conditions remain to be evaluated.

choices.text: The hospital can ignore pharmacist final validation because the product is not sold through retail pharmacies.
choices.why: Incorrect. Unavailability at retail does not remove pharmacist dispensing responsibilities.

choices.text: The prescription must still be valid and issued by an appropriately authorized practitioner; retail unavailability is not a waiver of those rules.
choices.why: Correct. Section 722.090(D) and applicable controlled-prescribing rules continue to apply to hospital dispensing.

questions.topic: Clinic cannot supply outpatient controlled drug if pharmacy services absent from facility license
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts clinic operates a licensed medical practice but does not have pharmacy services listed on its health-facility license. A clinic practitioner lawfully orders a Schedule VI medicine and asks the clinic to send a 30-day supply
questions.legal_decision: Separate lawful immediate clinic administration from dispensing take-home controlled medications without clinic pharmacy authorization.
questions.critical_exception: Facility health license omits pharmacy services and no c94C §9(e) authorization.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If pharmacy services were listed on the clinic health license and other prerequisites were met, take-home dispensing to eligible clinic patients could be authorized.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts clinic operates a licensed medical practice but does not have pharmacy services listed on its health-facility license. A clinic practitioner lawfully orders a Schedule VI medicine and asks the clinic to send a 30-day supply home with the patient. Another dose could instead be given in the clinic for immediate administration. No separate authorization under M.G.L. c.94C §9(e) is available. Which action is lawful under 105 CMR 722.091(B)?

choices.text: Give the patient the 30-day take-home supply because the prescribing clinician is employed by the clinic.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 722.091(B) independently restricts a clinic without pharmacy services on its facility license from dispensing non-immediate controlled medicines.

choices.text: Do not dispense the 30-day take-home supply from this clinic; authorized immediate administration is the express exception.
choices.why: Correct. Section 722.091(B) bars controlled-substance dispensing beyond immediate administration unless pharmacy services are on the facility license or other §9(e) authority applies.

choices.text: Let an unlicensed office receptionist dispense the same take-home supply to avoid the clinic pharmacy issue.
choices.why: Incorrect. Staff delegation cannot create facility-level dispensing authorization.

choices.text: Mark the 30-day outpatient package 'immediate administration' and permit the patient to take the remainder home.
choices.why: Incorrect. A label does not turn a take-home supply into immediate clinical administration.

choices.text: Ask the patient to waive the state's facility-pharmacy licensing requirement by signing an informed consent.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient consent does not waive 105 CMR 722.091(B).

questions.topic: Clinic pharmacy prescription must be from clinic practitioner for current registered patient
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts licensed clinic pharmacy that is not registered as a retail drug store receives an outpatient Schedule VI prescription for a person formally registered as a current clinic patient. The written prescription comes from a physi
questions.legal_decision: Require clinic pharmacy prescriptions to fall within both authorized clinic practitioner and recipient classes.
questions.critical_exception: Patient is clinic-registered, but prescriber is entirely outside clinic and no retail license applies.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the original prescription were issued by an authorized practitioner of the clinic for the current clinic patient, the specific clinic-prescriber limitation would be satisfied.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts licensed clinic pharmacy that is not registered as a retail drug store receives an outpatient Schedule VI prescription for a person formally registered as a current clinic patient. The written prescription comes from a physician in an unrelated independent private practice, not a practitioner of this clinic. No separate retail pharmacy license or special exemption is present. Which steps reflect 105 CMR 722.091(A)? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The clinic pharmacy may fill the prescription solely because the patient is currently registered there, irrespective of which practice wrote it.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 722.091(A) couples clinic patients/employees with a prescription issued by a legally authorized clinic practitioner.

choices.text: Any unrelated private physician becomes a clinic practitioner merely by writing a prescription for a clinic patient.
choices.why: Incorrect. External prescriber status does not automatically satisfy the clinic practitioner limitation.

choices.text: Do not fill the outside prescriber's take-home order under ordinary clinic-pharmacy authority without an appropriate independent basis.
choices.why: Correct. The clinic pharmacy's outpatient dispensing authority is defined in 722.091(A) and is limited to its specified prescribers and recipients.

choices.text: Arrange lawful fulfillment through an appropriately licensed retail pharmacy or obtain an eligible clinic practitioner's authorized prescription if clinically appropriate.
choices.why: Correct. These are viable ways to address the identified prescriber/facility authority mismatch without inventing dispensing powers.

choices.text: Treat the clinic as a hospital outpatient pharmacy and apply a 14-day hospital-discharge cap to make the outside prescription legal.
choices.why: Incorrect. The clinic pharmacy's authority under 722.091 is different from the hospital ED/discharge rule of 722.090(B).

questions.topic: Hospital formulary interchange must honor prescriber no-substitution instruction
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy fills otherwise valid prescriptions for two current hospital outpatients. On Rx X the authorized practitioner writes 'no substitution' for the brand; on Rx Y the practitioner does not indicate no substituti
questions.legal_decision: Honor no-substitution and use FDA therapeutically equivalent lower-priced hospital formulary product absent restriction.
questions.critical_exception: Current hospital outpatients, approved hospital formulary with FDA TE products and true price difference.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the prescriber also marked Rx Y no substitution, the ordinary 722.090(E) formulary interchange would no longer be allowed.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy fills otherwise valid prescriptions for two current hospital outpatients. On Rx X the authorized practitioner writes 'no substitution' for the brand; on Rx Y the practitioner does not indicate no substitution and the hospital's approved formulary lists a less expensive FDA-therapeutically-equivalent generic. Which dispensing actions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Interchange Rx X because the hospital's formulary is more authoritative than a prescriber's no-substitution instruction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 722.090(E) requires the hospital pharmacy to dispense the prescribed drug when no substitution is indicated.

choices.text: Dispense the prescribed product for Rx X unless a separate lawfully applicable exception authorizes a different outcome.
choices.why: Correct. Hospital rule 105 CMR 722.090(E) directly respects the prescriber's no-substitution choice.

choices.text: Dispense an unapproved, nontherapeutically-equivalent hospital-preferred product for Rx Y simply because it is cheaper.
choices.why: Incorrect. The hospital formulary is limited to FDA therapeutically equivalent drugs.

choices.text: Dispense the lower-priced therapeutically equivalent formulary product for Rx Y when no substitution was not indicated.
choices.why: Correct. Section 722.090(E) directs selection of the less expensive hospital-formulary drug absent no-substitution.

choices.text: Assume all retail pharmacy substitution labels under 247 CMR 9.05 necessarily replace the distinct hospital-formulary provisions.
choices.why: Incorrect. Hospital dispensing is independently governed by 105 CMR 722.090(E); do not automatically transplant retail-only provisions.

questions.topic: Admitted inpatient transferred before overnight still qualifies as hospital inpatient
questions.trigger: A patient is formally admitted to a Massachusetts hospital as an inpatient at 4 PM, but a medical emergency requires transfer to another hospital at 8 PM before the patient has spent a night in an inpatient bed. The hospital pharmacist must
questions.legal_decision: Preserve original hospital inpatient status for formally admitted patient medically transferred before overnight.
questions.critical_exception: Formal inpatient admission occurred before the medically required same-day transfer.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the person was seen only in the ED and never formally admitted as an inpatient, this special inpatient definition would not apply.
questions.stem: A patient is formally admitted to a Massachusetts hospital as an inpatient at 4 PM, but a medical emergency requires transfer to another hospital at 8 PM before the patient has spent a night in an inpatient bed. The hospital pharmacist must classify the patient's medication order under 105 CMR 722.020 and 722.090. Staff argue the patient must be treated as an ED discharge outpatient because no overnight stay occurred. What is the correct classification?

choices.text: An ED discharge patient by definition whenever the actual admission lasts less than 24 hours.
choices.why: Incorrect. The regulation expressly preserves inpatient status after formal admission if discharge or transfer for medical reasons occurs before an overnight stay.

choices.text: Not a hospital patient at all because the receiving hospital, not the original hospital, will complete treatment.
choices.why: Incorrect. The original hospital formally admitted and treated the patient before transfer.

choices.text: A hospital outpatient because every transferred inpatient is automatically reclassified retroactively under the 14-day discharge prescription rule.
choices.why: Incorrect. Transfer after formal inpatient admission does not automatically change the original inpatient classification.

choices.text: A clinic employee because the patient did not remain in bed overnight.
choices.why: Incorrect. Hospital inpatient classification depends on admission and transfer circumstances, not employee status.

choices.text: A hospital inpatient under the special definition for a formally admitted person transferred for medical reasons before an overnight stay.
choices.why: Correct. 105 CMR 722.020 explicitly includes formally admitted patients transferred to another hospital before occupying an inpatient bed overnight.

questions.topic: Prospective DUR finds age-related contraindication despite insurer authorization
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a newly issued, electronically signed medication order for a pediatric patient. The payer approves the claim, and the computer shows no interaction alert. Reviewing the patient's age and the proposed medi
questions.legal_decision: Investigate and document clinical age-related contraindication independently of insurer or computer alerts.
questions.critical_exception: A new prescription, positive clinically significant age contraindication found by pharmacist, no computer alert.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If documented assessment and prescriber clarification established a safe, appropriate regimen, the pharmacist could dispense after resolving the identified problem.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacist receives a newly issued, electronically signed medication order for a pediatric patient. The payer approves the claim, and the computer shows no interaction alert. Reviewing the patient's age and the proposed medication, the pharmacist independently identifies a clinically significant age-related contraindication. The technician says the insurer's authorization removes any need to ask the prescriber. Which action complies with the pharmacist's prospective DUR duty?

choices.text: Release the medication because claims approval legally certifies pediatric suitability for dispensing.
choices.why: Incorrect. Coverage approval is not clinical approval and does not displace pharmacist prospective DUR.

choices.text: Have a technician suppress the age information so the clinical profile no longer conflicts with the prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Suppression of relevant age history undermines prospective DUR and professional responsibility.

choices.text: Evaluate and resolve the age-specific risk before dispensing, obtain clarification as necessary, and document measures taken.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.17(1)(j),(2) requires reasonable effort to identify age-related contraindications and document appropriate resolution.

choices.text: Wait until the patient's next refill for the first DUR assessment because electronically signed orders have been authenticated.
choices.why: Incorrect. The prospective assessment is required before each new order is dispensed or delivered.

choices.text: Change the medication's manufacturer NDC without clinical review so the order no longer looks age-contraindicated in software.
choices.why: Incorrect. Replacing the NDC does not address the clinician's identified age-related risk.

questions.topic: Hospital pharmacy employee family eligibility depends on same-household residency
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy holds a hospital pharmacy license but no retail Drug Store Pharmacy license. An employee wants it to dispense an ordinary outpatient prescription for the employee's 27-year-old son, who lives in an apartmen
questions.legal_decision: Decline hospital pharmacy outpatient dispensing to nonpatient adult child living outside employee household.
questions.critical_exception: Child not a hospital patient and does not live with employee, hospital holds no Drug Store retail license.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the adult son lived in the employee's same household and met the remaining requirements, the family-recipient exception could apply.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital pharmacy holds a hospital pharmacy license but no retail Drug Store Pharmacy license. An employee wants it to dispense an ordinary outpatient prescription for the employee's 27-year-old son, who lives in an apartment across town and is neither a hospital patient nor employed at the hospital. The family relationship is authentic, and the prescriber is properly authorized. Does the hospital employee-family exception allow the hospital pharmacy to fill it?

choices.text: Yes; any adult child of any hospital employee is eligible without regard to residence or patient status.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.01(13) defines the allowed employees' children as those living in the same household.

choices.text: Yes, because an authorized outside prescriber can convert a hospital pharmacy into a retail dispensing facility.
choices.why: Incorrect. Prescriber authority does not expand the pharmacy facility license's recipient restrictions.

choices.text: Yes, if the pharmacist charges the hospital's employee discount even though the son lives separately.
choices.why: Incorrect. Pricing does not cure an ineligible recipient under the hospital-only license.

choices.text: No; this nonpatient adult child lives outside the employee's household and is not independently within the hospital pharmacy's permitted recipients.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.01(13) includes employees' children only when residing in the same household, absent other patient status or separate retail license.

choices.text: No, because hospital pharmacies may never dispense any outpatient prescription to an employee or an eligible family member.
choices.why: Incorrect. Hospital pharmacies have a limited exception for employees, spouses and same-household children.

questions.citation: 247 CMR 9.01(13); 105 CMR 722.020 definition of Hospital Employees

questions.topic: Hospital controlled-nursing-unit records need weekly QA independent of double lock
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts hospital central pharmacy supplies prescribed controlled medications to a staffed nursing unit. Each Schedule II–V dose is maintained in the double-locked cabinet and entered in a perpetual inventory, and waste events are ap
questions.legal_decision: Perform documented at-least-weekly QA review of controlled-drug administration, independently of secure stock and individual patient chart entries.
questions.critical_exception: The nursing unit has proper per-dose records and storage but skips weekly management QA.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If management completed and documented compliant weekly QA, this specific oversight deficiency would be removed.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts hospital central pharmacy supplies prescribed controlled medications to a staffed nursing unit. Each Schedule II–V dose is maintained in the double-locked cabinet and entered in a perpetual inventory, and waste events are appropriately co-signed. The nursing director proposes skipping any weekly pharmacy/nursing review of medications ADMINISTERED because individual nurses already sign each administration record. Which steps follow current DPH hospital and clinic accountability guidance? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Conduct and document a quality-assurance review of administered Schedule II–VI controlled drugs at least weekly by pharmacy/nursing management.
choices.why: Correct. DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Hospitals/Clinics with Pharmacies, 'Nursing Units—General,' require QA review of all Schedules II–VI medications administered at least weekly.

choices.text: Assume each individual administration entry eliminates the facility's separate weekly management QA requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Recording doses and weekly management QA serve different purposes and are separately required by the guidance.

choices.text: Continue maintaining controlled stock security and access to authorized licensed staff, notwithstanding completion of the weekly QA review.
choices.why: Correct. The same guidelines require authorized licensed access plus accountability; QA does not substitute for secure storage.

choices.text: Allow a hospital security guard who is not licensed to independently dispose of Schedule II drug waste because a weekly QA audit is planned.
choices.why: Incorrect. The guidance requires appropriate licensed staff for controlled waste; later QA does not authorize unlicensed waste.

choices.text: Review Schedule II stock only once a year because the hospital uses perpetual records for every individual dose.
choices.why: Incorrect. The weekly QA management review specifically applies to all Schedules II–VI medications administered.

questions.citation: DPH General Accountability Guidelines for Controlled Substances in Hospitals/Clinics with Pharmacies, Nursing Units—General; compare 105 CMR 700.000

questions.topic: Schedule VI electronic files must be separately retrievable even if not DEA scheduled
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy stores all Schedule VI prescriptions electronically in the same unsorted data table as nonprescription sales receipts. The system can display a patient's fill history, but cannot separately retrieve or export
questions.legal_decision: Keep electronically separable MA Schedule VI prescription records rather than relying on a merged unfilterable transaction table.
questions.critical_exception: Only SVI electronic separability is missing; other general electronic patient-profile functions work.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the pharmacy's records already supported separately retrieving and displaying Schedule VI prescriptions, this particular recordkeeping defect would be cured.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacy stores all Schedule VI prescriptions electronically in the same unsorted data table as nonprescription sales receipts. The system can display a patient's fill history, but cannot separately retrieve or export its Schedule VI prescriptions as a class for inspection. The pharmacy manager argues that electronic segregation rules apply only to DEA Schedules II–V. What must change?

choices.text: No change is needed because federally unscheduled prescriptions never need state record separation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Massachusetts explicitly regulates Schedule VI prescriptions separately from federally controlled prescriptions.

choices.text: Make the electronic Schedule VI prescription records separately retrievable while preserving ordinary record and patient-profile duties.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.16(4) requires paper SVI prescriptions to be segregated and electronic SVI prescriptions to be electronically separable.

choices.text: Delete all Schedule VI prescription history after the patient's first refill because its original paper is not subject to a DEA filing requirement.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.16(1) requires prescription records to be maintained for at least two years and does not waive that for Schedule VI.

choices.text: Transfer all Schedule VI prescriptions to the pharmacy's federal Schedule II separate paper filing cabinet to avoid digital changes.
choices.why: Incorrect. Separate federal Schedule II records are not the required Schedule VI grouping.

choices.text: List Schedule VI products as OTC transactions in the database so inspectors will not request controlled-substance records.
choices.why: Incorrect. Misrepresenting prescription dispensing as OTC sales violates accurate recordkeeping.

questions.topic: Emergency oral Schedule II written follow-up never arrives: pharmacist must notify DEA
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist properly dispensed an emergency-period Schedule II medication after directly taking a qualifying oral order from an authorized prescriber. The pharmacist documented and reduced the oral order to writing as
questions.legal_decision: Report missing seven-calendar-day emergency CII signed follow-up to DEA, preserving original oral record.
questions.critical_exception: Compliant emergency CII oral fill already occurred; prescriber fails to furnish the seven-day signed follow-up.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the signed follow-up were timely delivered or appropriately postmarked and linked to the record, the separate failure-to-furnish DEA notice would not be triggered.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts retail pharmacist properly dispensed an emergency-period Schedule II medication after directly taking a qualifying oral order from an authorized prescriber. The pharmacist documented and reduced the oral order to writing as required. Seven CALENDAR days pass, and the prescribing practitioner has not delivered or properly mailed the required signed follow-up prescription. The patient was treated appropriately and no new medication is being requested. What must the pharmacist do under federal law? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Simply close the record, because the seven-day deadline applies only to the prescriber and cannot impose a pharmacist action.
choices.why: Incorrect. 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(4) specifically requires the pharmacist to notify DEA if the prescriber fails to supply the follow-up.

choices.text: Create a fictitious written order dated within the seven-day window and sign the prescriber's name to resolve the missing document.
choices.why: Incorrect. Fabrication of a prescription is unlawful and does not satisfy §1306.11(d)(4).

choices.text: Notify the nearest DEA Diversion Field Office that the required emergency Schedule II follow-up was not furnished.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.11(d)(4) expressly requires the pharmacist to notify the nearest DEA office of the failed follow-up.

choices.text: Assume telephone verification of the prescriber's DEA number substitutes indefinitely for the missing seven-day paper/electronic follow-up.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verification is required independently of the written follow-up obligation.

choices.text: Retain the properly documented original emergency oral authorization and its compliance history while addressing the missing follow-up.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1306.11(d)(2),(4) requires the oral order to be reduced to a written record and linked with the subsequent documentation, or retained with the failure and required notice.

questions.citation: 21 CFR 1306.11(d)(2)–(4); DEA Practitioner's Manual, emergency prescribing

questions.topic: Prospective DUR identifies probable undertreatment without software warning
questions.trigger: A patient picking up a new maintenance medicine tells a Massachusetts pharmacist that the physician intentionally doubled the dose last week, but the newly issued prescription still lists the older lower dose and the directions may leave th
questions.legal_decision: Resolve likely underutilization and conflicting dosing before filling; document pharmacist clinical intervention.
questions.critical_exception: Patient-reported recent dose change conflicts with current new prescription; correctness unresolved.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If a reliable prescriber clarification established the current lower dose was deliberate, the pharmacist could document the resolution and dispense the verified therapy.
questions.stem: A patient picking up a new maintenance medicine tells a Massachusetts pharmacist that the physician intentionally doubled the dose last week, but the newly issued prescription still lists the older lower dose and the directions may leave the patient substantially undertreated. There is no insurance or computer alert, and the pharmacist cannot confirm whether the current order or the patient's account is correct. The technician proposes dispensing the lower-dose label without inquiry because underutilization is not a drug interaction. What is the best step?

choices.text: Dispense immediately because prospective DUR concerns only drug–drug interactions and controlled-substance misuse.
choices.why: Incorrect. 247 CMR 9.17(1)(a),(f),(i) includes underutilization, dosage, and significant changes in drug or dose.

choices.text: Have the technician increase the dose on the prescription without prescriber confirmation as a non-discretionary data correction.
choices.why: Incorrect. Unconfirmed clinical dose modification is not a technician clerical act.

choices.text: Tell the patient to take extra doses from the bottle and ignore the written instructions, without documenting any change.
choices.why: Incorrect. Verbal unverified dosing contradicting the order creates risk and violates prospective DUR expectations.

choices.text: Clarify the intended dose with the patient and/or prescriber as clinically appropriate, then document the pharmacist's DUR response before dispensing.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.17(1)(a),(f),(i),(2) requires prospective assessment of potential underutilization and material dose discrepancies, followed by appropriate documented action.

choices.text: Delete the old dose from all electronic records and treat the patient's recalled regimen as the verified new order.
choices.why: Incorrect. Erasing history without determining prescriber intent does not satisfy verification or DUR.

questions.topic: Pharmacy purchasing and disposal records: separate retention from serious QRE ledger
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts community pharmacy maintains pharmacy-generated controlled-substance purchasing and return invoices and drug-disposal records. A manager proposes retaining prescription records for two years but deleting purchase and disposa
questions.legal_decision: Retain readily retrievable purchasing, return and disposal/destruction documents for at least two years.
questions.critical_exception: Ordinary pharmacy records, no qualifying longer federal or payor retention requirement assumed.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If all required records had been preserved and retrievable for at least two years, the described premature destruction would not occur.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts community pharmacy maintains pharmacy-generated controlled-substance purchasing and return invoices and drug-disposal records. A manager proposes retaining prescription records for two years but deleting purchase and disposal records after only 15 months, saying the two-year record rule concerns prescriptions exclusively. No longer federal, payor, or special-reporting retention requirement is relevant to this question. Which conclusions follow 247 CMR 9.16? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: Purchasing, return, disposal, and destruction records must also be readily retrievable for at least two years.
choices.why: Correct. 247 CMR 9.16(1) expressly lists prescription records, purchasing and return records, and disposal and destruction records together.

choices.text: The pharmacy can eliminate purchasing and disposal records after one year because only printed prescription copies are regulated.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.16(1) sets the same at-least-two-year minimum for the listed purchasing and disposal records.

choices.text: The pharmacy should preserve those records for at least the applicable two years, with longer controlling obligations still respected if they exist.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.16(1) is a minimum; the stipulated case has no additional rule but other authorities may impose longer retention in other cases.

choices.text: Patient confidentiality allows the pharmacy to erase controlled drug receipts without documenting the actual destruction or returns.
choices.why: Incorrect. Confidentiality does not extinguish separate inventory and transaction recordkeeping.

choices.text: The manufacturer must preserve all pharmacy buying records, so the dispensing pharmacy can delete its local retention copies after 15 months.
choices.why: Incorrect. Records kept by a supplier do not waive the pharmacy's own 247 CMR 9.16(1) obligation.

questions.topic: Pharmacy initiates a patient-requested prescription transfer as patient's agent
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts patient asks the receiving pharmacy to obtain the remaining authorized refills of an ordinary Schedule VI maintenance prescription from the former pharmacy. Both are appropriately licensed and the original is still within it
questions.legal_decision: Permit receiving pharmacy to act as patient agent and effectuate timely transfer without extra direct patient call.
questions.critical_exception: Patient authorization verified, original VI prescription has valid remaining refills and is within issuance window.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the patient had expressly refused a transfer and given no agent authorization, the receiving pharmacy could not claim patient-requested transfer authority.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts patient asks the receiving pharmacy to obtain the remaining authorized refills of an ordinary Schedule VI maintenance prescription from the former pharmacy. Both are appropriately licensed and the original is still within its one-year validity. The former pharmacy refuses unless the patient personally calls the transferring pharmacist a second time, even though it has independently confirmed that the patient authorized the receiving pharmacist to act. The former pharmacy intends to delay transfer for a week. What is the correct conclusion under 247 CMR 9.14?

choices.text: A receiving pharmacist can never act as a patient's agent for a transfer; only a notarized patient request is sufficient.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.14(2) expressly permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent to facilitate a transfer.

choices.text: The receiving pharmacy may act on the patient's verified request as their agent, and the former pharmacy must transfer timely to avoid delaying care.
choices.why: Correct. Sections 9.14(1)–(2) authorize the pharmacy as patient's agent and require timely transfer at patient/agent request.

choices.text: The original pharmacy must wait seven days after a verified request before another pharmacy may use the original prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.14(1) has a prompt transfer obligation; it does not impose a default seven-day waiting period.

choices.text: An otherwise valid prescription becomes invalid solely because the patient authorized another pharmacy to arrange its transfer.
choices.why: Incorrect. Patient agency does not invalidate an otherwise valid transferable prescription.

choices.text: The former pharmacy may charge a penalty for pharmacy-agent transfers even though ordinary patient direct requests have no transfer fee.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.14(3) expressly prohibits fees for prescription transfer.

questions.topic: Multi-dose adherence packaging must be tamper-evident and not reclosable
questions.trigger: A Massachusetts pharmacy designs a compliance packaging product holding individually identified daily solid-oral medicine doses. The pouches meet medication compatibility, supply-duration, drug-schedule and labeling requirements, but the se
questions.legal_decision: Reject reclosable, unnoticeably opened compliance packaging and nonpermanent drug labels.
questions.critical_exception: Even though all other compliance packaging safeguards are assumed to be satisfied, (1)(e) fails.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the package were changed to show opening, prevent reclosure, and keep labels from being altered/removed, this defect would be cured.
questions.stem: A Massachusetts pharmacy designs a compliance packaging product holding individually identified daily solid-oral medicine doses. The pouches meet medication compatibility, supply-duration, drug-schedule and labeling requirements, but the sealing system allows a patient or staff member to open a cell, reclose it invisibly, and remove or replace the medication-information label without leaving evidence. The designer proposes using it anyway because the packages are not child-resistant bottles. What must change?

choices.text: Approve the package because tamper-evident closures are required only for controlled substances in Schedules II–V.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 9.08(1)(e) applies to compliance packaging regardless of controlled schedule.

choices.text: Leave the closure unchanged if the pharmacist photographs each filled cell before shipment; photographs create the required physical tamper evidence.
choices.why: Incorrect. Photography cannot substitute for a design that visibly shows opening and prevents unnoticeable reclosure or label removal.

choices.text: Change only the beyond-use date to seven days; that automatically makes the physical closure acceptable.
choices.why: Incorrect. BUD assignment does not cure the independent packaging design requirements.

choices.text: Replace the patient name with an alphanumeric code so that removal of the detachable label cannot misidentify a prescription.
choices.why: Incorrect. De-identifying the package cannot waive patient-specific labeling and tamper-evidence requirements.

choices.text: Use packaging designed to show opening, prevent reclosure, and prevent removable or alterable medication labels.
choices.why: Correct. Section 9.08(1)(e) expressly requires tamper evidence, non-reclosable design and a label that cannot be altered or removed.

questions.topic: DEA Form 222 POA revoked by current registration signer with two witnesses
questions.actor: DEA registrant signing officer; departing purchasing manager
questions.trigger: A DEA-registered Massachusetts pharmacy previously granted a valid power of attorney (POA) to its purchasing manager to execute Schedule II DEA Form 222 orders. The corporate officer who signed the pharmacy's most recent DEA registration ap
questions.legal_decision: Properly revoke order-form POA with authorized signer and two witnesses; retain inspectable record.
questions.critical_exception: One witness only and an unexecuted revocation memo; purchasing manager has left.
questions.counterfactual_flip: If the last DEA application signatory signed a revocation witnessed by two individuals and records were retained, the POA would no longer authorize new orders.
questions.stem: A DEA-registered Massachusetts pharmacy previously granted a valid power of attorney (POA) to its purchasing manager to execute Schedule II DEA Form 222 orders. The corporate officer who signed the pharmacy's most recent DEA registration application now wants to revoke that POA after the purchasing manager leaves. Only one employee is available to witness a revocation memo, but management intends to file it without a second witness and use the POA to process another order. Which federal conclusions are correct? SELECT ALL THAT APPLY.

choices.text: The person who signed the latest DEA application or reregistration may revoke the POA, but two witnesses must sign the revocation.
choices.why: Correct. 21 CFR 1305.05(e) governs who can revoke and requires two witness signatures.

choices.text: An informal unsigned phone instruction from the corporate finance department automatically replaces the required witnessed revocation instrument.
choices.why: Incorrect. Section 1305.05(e) requires a revocation signed by the authorized person and two witnesses.

choices.text: An individual with a revoked POA may continue to sign new Form 222 orders indefinitely until DEA separately mails a pharmacist renewal notice.
choices.why: Incorrect. Revocation terminates the delegated ordering authority; DEA does not require an unrelated pharmacist renewal notice.

choices.text: The POA and properly documented revocation must be retained with the registrant's executed Forms 222 records and available for inspection.
choices.why: Correct. Section 1305.05(a),(e) requires POA documentation and proper retention with controlled substance order records.

choices.text: A departed manager's national pharmacy certification automatically keeps the ordering POA valid even after an executed revocation.
choices.why: Incorrect. Ordering rights arise from the registrant's executed POA, not technician certification.
